title: Is BRICS Losing Its Mojo?
gist: Ahead of BRICS's September 12 New Delhi summit, the bloc's rapid 2023-25 expansion to 10 members has produced repeated failures to issue joint statements amid intra-bloc splits (Egypt/Ethiopia vs. South Africa on UNSC reform, Iran vs. UAE over the 2026 U.S.-Israel-Iran war), even as BRICS has overtaken the G-7 in economic output and its New Development Bank keeps functioning with strong credit ratings.

themes.theme: BRICS's economic scale and institutional success

insights.claim: BRICS has overtaken the G-7 in terms of economic output and become the first truly transcontinental club outside the wealthy West, spanning all regions of the global south after its 2023-25 expansion added Egypt, Ethiopia, Indonesia, Iran, and the United Arab Emirates to the original five (Brazil, Russia, India, China, South Africa), plus a lower tier of 10 'partner countries.'
insights.speaker: Sarang Shidore
insights.so_what: BRICS's aggregate economic weight now exceeding the G-7 is a structural signal that global economic gravity has shifted toward this bloc, relevant for long-term positioning in emerging-market and multipolar-order theses.
insights.locator: It now includes all regions of the global south and has overtaken the G-7

insights.claim: The New Development Bank, BRICS's flagship financial institution, has been operating for a decade with high credit ratings, making it the bloc's clearest concrete success story to date.
insights.speaker: Sarang Shidore
insights.so_what: The NDB is the most investable, functioning piece of BRICS institutional infrastructure and a reference point for tracking non-Western development finance flows as an alternative to World Bank/IMF-led lending.
insights.locator: Development finance is among its clearest success stories

insights.claim: New members Egypt and Ethiopia refused to endorse South Africa's bid for a reformed UN Security Council seat despite an apparent prior commitment to do so, causing BRICS foreign ministers' meetings to fail to issue joint statements in both September 2024 and April 2025—the first such failures in the bloc's history—and the 2025 Rio summit declaration ultimately dropped South Africa from its UNSC reform paragraph.
insights.speaker: Sarang Shidore
insights.so_what: First-ever joint-statement failures signal that BRICS's expanded membership has genuinely fractured internal cohesion, not just added optical complexity—a leading indicator that further expansion could paralyze consensus entirely.
insights.locator: In September 2024, a foreign ministers' meeting failed to issue a joint statement

insights.claim: The 2026 U.S.-Israel-Iran war (which also drew in the UAE) caused a second consecutive BRICS foreign ministers' meeting (May 2026) to fail to produce a joint statement, with Iran demanding that BRICS's terrorism condemnations also cover what it calls 'state terrorism' by the U.S. and Israel—a demand most other members rejected, forcing India to issue only a chair's statement instead of a consensus document.
insights.speaker: Sarang Shidore
insights.so_what: Direct member-state involvement in an active war (Iran, UAE) is now actively breaking BRICS consensus mechanisms—a template for how future regional conflicts drawing in multiple BRICS members will likely paralyze the bloc's collective statements.
insights.locator: The BRICS foreign ministers meeting in May 2026 again failed

insights.claim: In January 2026, South Africa hosted a naval drill with China, Iran, and Russia framed as a BRICS exercise, but India pointedly stayed away calling it 'entirely a South African initiative,' the UAE sent a ship but kept it docked, and Iran's participation drew sharp U.S. criticism—leading South Africa to order the Iranians excluded (who reportedly did not leave) and to investigate its own navy for insubordination.
insights.speaker: Sarang Shidore
insights.so_what: A vivid case study of BRICS members' divergent risk tolerance toward Iran-linked security cooperation—India's explicit distancing signals it will not let joint military symbolism drag it into confrontation with Washington.

themes.theme: Security has always been part of BRICS, contrary to a 'purely economic' framing

insights.claim: New research aggregating data across all 16 BRICS summit declarations to date shows that while economic development is the top focus area, geopolitical and security issues are a close second—meaning it is 'too late' and 'impractical' to try to de-securitize the BRICS agenda now, contrary to hopes that the bloc could retreat to a purely economic mandate.
insights.speaker: Sarang Shidore
insights.so_what: Investors/analysts hoping BRICS could shed geopolitical risk and function as a pure development-finance bloc should recalibrate—security friction is structurally embedded in the bloc's DNA, not a recent aberration.
insights.quote: It is simply too late to de-securitize the BRICS agenda. It is also impractical in our times when everything seems to be securitized.
insights.locator: New research aggregating data across all its summits

insights.claim: BRICS has always mixed security themes into its agenda since inception—multipolar order, UNSC reform, and anti-terrorism opposition appeared in its first 2009 leaders' summit and have recurred across all 16 subsequent summit declarations, including a 2011 paragraph on NATO's Libya intervention and 2012 references to the Arab-Israeli conflict, Syria, and Afghanistan.
insights.speaker: Sarang Shidore
insights.so_what: Historical continuity argument: the bloc's 2026 security-driven paralysis is a scaling-up of a longstanding structural feature, not a new phenomenon—useful for calibrating expectations about future summit dysfunction as membership grows further.
insights.locator: even during its first leaders' summit in 2009

themes.theme: Prescription: scale back security ambition, scale up delivery

insights.claim: The author argues BRICS should not attempt to take a position on every conflict, especially where such positions are unlikely to produce action, but should instead focus its security agenda narrowly on issues with the deepest buy-in across members, specifically countering nonstate violence—terrorism, piracy, and organized crime—which are 'serious and only multiplying.'
insights.speaker: Sarang Shidore
insights.so_what: A concrete prioritization framework for what BRICS security cooperation could plausibly deliver near-term (counter-piracy, counter-organized-crime) versus what will keep failing (great-power conflict positioning)—useful for gauging which BRICS security initiatives merit attention versus which are performative.
insights.locator: There is no need to take a position on every single raging war

insights.claim: BRICS quietly functions as a forum for easing bilateral tensions between members—the 2024 Kazan summit served as an important venue for India and China to de-escalate tensions that had spiked after their 2020 border clash.
insights.speaker: Sarang Shidore
insights.so_what: An underappreciated function of BRICS is as an off-ramp for bilateral great-power friction between members (e.g., India-China), which could matter for de-escalation dynamics beyond the bloc's formal joint communiqués.
insights.locator: BRICS also quietly serves as a forum

insights.claim: The author's overall thesis is that BRICS needs a 'third wind'—following the New Development Bank's founding (2012-14) and the 2023 membership expansion as its first two positive inflection points—built on delivering real developmental impact for the global south rather than further security entanglement, to avoid paralysis in an increasingly conflictual world.
insights.speaker: Sarang Shidore
insights.so_what: Sets a forward-looking marker: watch for a concrete developmental-finance scale-up initiative at or after the New Delhi summit as the signal BRICS is finding its 'third wind' rather than drifting into irrelevance.
insights.locator: To avert paralysis and stay relevant
